facts.query: How do locust swarms get so big so fast?
facts.explanation: After good rains, desert locusts breed in damp sand and each generation can be many times larger than the last. Within a few generations a modest outbreak can become a swarm dense enough to blanket a square kilometre and strip crops as it travels.

facts.query: How does a caterpillar turn into a butterfly?
facts.explanation: Monarch butterflies go through complete metamorphosis. A tiny egg hatches into a caterpillar that does nothing but eat milkweed and grow, then it forms a chrysalis in which its body is rebuilt into a winged adult that starts the cycle again.

facts.label: Egg
facts.title: Egg
facts.description: A female lays single eggs on the underside of milkweed leaves; each hatches after a few days.
facts.sourceNote: US Forest Service, Monarch butterfly life cycle

facts.label: Caterpillar
facts.title: Caterpillar (larva)
facts.description: The caterpillar eats milkweed almost nonstop, molting its skin several times as it grows over about two weeks.
facts.sourceNote: US Forest Service, Monarch butterfly life cycle

facts.label: Chrysalis
facts.title: Chrysalis (pupa)
facts.description: It hangs upside down and forms a green chrysalis, inside which its body is broken down and rebuilt.
facts.sourceNote: US Forest Service, Monarch butterfly life cycle

facts.label: Butterfly
facts.title: Adult butterfly
facts.description: The butterfly emerges, dries its wings, feeds on nectar, mates and lays eggs; the late-summer generation migrates south.
